query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a thin, ordered NiAl (B2 phase) interlayer between HEA layers will enable tuning of interface coherency such that, under high-temperature creep conditions, the dominant deformation mechanism transitions from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers composed solely of HEA layers with inherent lattice distortions and relatively uncontrolled interface coherency.
generation.intervention: Introduce a tunable, thin NiAl interlayer via controlled deposition to create coherent interfaces with the adjacent HEA layers.
generation.conditions: High-temperature creep testing environments (e.g., temperatures above 700 °C and under applied stresses where both long-range diffusion and dislocation motion are active).
generation.structural_mediator: The NiAl ordered B2 phase interlayer, which forms a coherent interface with the HEA layers, serves as the mediator between diffusion-controlled and dislocation-controlled creep regimes.
generation.mechanism: The coherent NiAl interlayer modifies the local atomic structure at the interface, lowering the diffusion barrier under conditions favoring atomic motion (thus promoting diffusion-mediated creep) and simultaneously acting as a barrier to dislocation nucleation under conditions favoring dislocation motion, thereby enabling a controlled shift between the two creep mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA multilayers with the NiAl interlayer will display a measurable transition in creep mechanism—from predominantly diffusion-mediated creep in one regime to dislocation-mediated creep in another—as the interface coherency is tuned via the NiAl layer thickness and processing parameters, contrasting with the baseline multilayers without the interlayer.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers without the NiAl interlayer, which are expected to lack a clearly defined transition between creep mechanisms due to uncontrolled interface coherency.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is predicted only within an optimal range of NiAl interlayer thickness and coherency. Excessively thick or poorly coherent interfaces may degrade overall mechanical performance or fail to mediate the intended creep mechanism transition.
generation.uncertainty: The exact transition conditions, optimal NiAl thickness, and quantifiable shifts in creep mechanism require systematic experimental and simulation studies for precise determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA multilayer samples: one set incorporating a NiAl interlayer with controlled thickness variations and one control set without the interlayer. Subject both sample sets to identical high-temperature creep tests under incrementally increased stress levels. Use in situ and post-test characterizations to monitor creep strain progression, dislocation activity, and interface structures.
measurements: Creep strain versus time curves under controlled high-temperature and stress conditions
High-resolution TEM and XRD analysis to quantify interface coherency and NiAl layer structure
TEM analysis of dislocation density and distribution within the HEA layers
Diffusion parameter measurements across the interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integration of the NiAl interlayer does not lead to a statistically significant and reproducible shift from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep compared to the control samples, or if varying the NiAl thickness does not correlate with changes in the creep mechanism, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. The physical metallurgy of superalloys [9] have been employed to design HEAs by utilization of significant volume fractions of stable and coherent L1 2 γ′ to provide high temperature strength, e.g., Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 HEA was designed to contain 46 vol% of γ′ precipitates [10] , and its tensile strength could surpass those of Inconel 617 and All

frame.system: High‐entropy alloy (HEA) multilayer coatings in which individual HEA layers—with their inherent lattice distortions—are separated by engineered interfaces (of variable coherency) that govern high‐temperature deformation.
frame.goal: To identify and rationalize a candidate transition material that can mediate between diffusion‐controlled (e.g., Nabarro–Herring or Coble) and dislocation‐controlled creep regimes, thereby helping to elucidate the role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers.
frame.limitation: The specific influence of interface coherency on the transition between diffusion‐mediated and dislocation‐mediated creep mechanisms is not well understood.
root_cause_cues: transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms
constraints: the material must be compatible with HEAs and maintain overall superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance
it should form interfaces whose coherency can be controlled or tuned
the selected material should function as an effective barrier (or mediator) that is sensitive to temperature and stress such that it promotes one mechanism over the other when desired
frame.regime: High-temperature creep conditions where both long-range atomic diffusion and dislocation motion are active, with stresses that promote a switch in the dominant deformation mechanism.
prior_attempts: Studies on HEA multilayers have modulated interface coherency but have not clearly identified a specific interlayer material that can serve as a tunable transition between different creep mechanisms.
Earlier work in simpler multilayer systems (e.g., Cu/Ni, or conventional alloys) has demonstrated the impact of interfacial structure on creep, yet did not address the unique challenges of HEAs.

decision.trend: Initial studies on HEAs (as in PMC7512559) explored high‐temperature creep by identifying diffusion‐assisted dislocation climb as the dominant mechanism in bulk or single‐phase HEAs. Later, work such as PMC11087546 highlighted that very coherent interfaces—achieved via engineered phase boundaries in multiphase or eutectic HEAs—can significantly alter deformation responses. Although interface coherency has been modulated in multilayer coatings, none of the studies have yet isolated a specific interlayer material that can act as a switch, mediating between diffusion‐controlled (e.g., Nabarro–Herring/Coble) and dislocation‐controlled creep in HEA multilayers.
decision.unsolved: The critical open question remains how to exploit and control interface coherency to enable a material interlayer that effectively facilitates a transition between diffusion‐mediated and dislocation‐mediated creep mechanisms while preserving the overall performance of HEA multilayers.
decision.lever: Integrate a thin NiAl (ordered B2 phase) interlayer with tunable thickness and deposition conditions to adjust the lattice coherency with adjacent HEA layers. Systematic studies should correlate interface structure (via in‐situ and advanced characterization) with high-temperature creep behavior.
decision.why: NiAl inherently forms a coherent, ordered B2 interface with many HEA matrices, offering an intermediate diffusion coefficient and modulated barrier for dislocation motion. This matches the need for a transition material that can preferentially promote diffusion-mediated creep at one set of conditions and dislocation-mediated creep at another, directly following the trend and addressing the gap identified in previous studies.
